global.headline: Houthi missiles burn Riyadh refinery as Saudi jets pound Sanaa
summary: Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the group hit an Aramco refinery south of Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones; an AFP journalist in the Saudi capital saw flames and smoke at the site, with firefighters, ambulances and police deployed. Saree called it a response to roughly 60 Saudi air and missile attacks in 24 hours.

Houthi-run Al-Masirah said Saudi aircraft struck Sanaa 26 times on Saturday, after Thursday night's first bombardment of the Yemeni capital since fighting resumed in July. The two sides have traded fire since the Houthis seized the whole of Yemen's Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab strait in a September offensive.
global.geopolitical: With Hormuz contested and Bab al-Mandab under Houthi control, both of the region's maritime chokepoints are now held or threatened by Iran-aligned forces — and Saudi Arabia, the war's most cautious large player, is bombing a capital again.
global.socioeconomic: Strikes on refining rather than export terminals hit the same scarce commodity the G7 just drew down reserves for: refined product. A sustained outage at Riyadh's refinery would tighten diesel further, days after the 100m-barrel release.

global.headline: Russia hits second Kyiv bridge, cutting the capital's river crossings
summary: A Russian strike on Saturday morning hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge over the Dnipro in Kyiv, injuring two people and tearing up the road surface and trolleybus power lines. Traffic from the east bank to the west was suspended. Russian forces also struck a logistics centre near the capital overnight.

It was the third consecutive day of attacks on Kyiv's river crossings: at least three drone strikes on 1 and 2 October damaged a support, a guardrail, the road surface and a metro protective barrier on the Southern Bridge, which was closed entirely. These are the first strikes of the war on Kyiv's Dnipro bridges.
global.geopolitical: Targeting bridges rather than substations is a new doctrine aimed at splitting a capital of three million into two halves, and it is harder to repair under repeat attack than the grid Moscow spent two winters hitting.
global.socioeconomic: Kyiv's left bank holds roughly a third of the city's residents and its commuter traffic depends on a handful of crossings. Losing two degrades labour mobility, freight and emergency response just as the heating season begins.

global.headline: US grants first sanctions carve-out of the war as UK case advances
summary: Iraq's prime minister Ali al-Zaidi said Washington granted an exemption letting Iranian carriers, excluding Mahan Air, run 40 daily flights into Najaf for pilgrims and medical travellers — the first US sanctions concession of the war, while the seven-day Hormuz plan stays stuck on sequencing.

In London, Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court over an alleged chlorine-bomb plot against Manchester's Jewish community, having scouted the Jewish Museum and Heaton Park Synagogue. Neither entered a plea; both were remanded to an Old Bailey hearing on 23 October. All six RAF Fairford suspects are now on bail without charge. At an Oklahoma rally, Trump newly claimed the Iranian nuclear sites he bombed were also "drug factories".
global.geopolitical: A narrow humanitarian waiver is the first thing Washington has given Tehran in seven months, and it was given to Baghdad rather than to Iran — relief routed through a third country, testing whether sequencing can be finessed instead of settled.
global.socioeconomic: Forty daily Najaf flights restore a pilgrimage economy worth hundreds of millions a year to Iraq and offer Iranians a sanctioned-airspace exit. The carve-out's design is now the template others will seek.

global.headline: Half a million march in Spain as Sánchez weighs a snap election
summary: Protesters filled Madrid and about 50 other cities on Saturday, a day after parliament voted down two emergency housing decrees. Government officials put the Madrid turnout at a minimum of 70,000; the capital's Tenants' Union claimed 500,000. Marchers called for a general strike and structural reform of the rental market.

The rejected decrees would have made tenancy contracts renew automatically and restricted evictions of vulnerable tenants. The crisis was catalysed by the forced removal of a pensioner from her Madrid flat on 23 September. Spanish media report Pedro Sánchez may call a November election, and that he was waiting to see Saturday's turnout before deciding.
global.geopolitical: A minority government that cannot pass a decree on its signature issue has no legislative path left; the only question is whether Sánchez picks the election date or has it forced on him by the next failed vote.
global.socioeconomic: Spanish rents have outrun wages for a decade and the decrees were the only near-term protection on offer. Their defeat leaves eviction proceedings running and makes housing the organising issue of a national campaign.

global.headline: UAE calls Flydubai cockpit attack terrorism; co-pilot was flagged in 2024
summary: The UAE's prosecutor general said the Flydubai co-pilot "attempted to carry out a terrorist act", using the cockpit's crash axe on captain Smit Machchhar before the Boeing 737 MAX 8 plunged from 34,000 feet on the Dubai–Tel Aviv run. He has been named as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national born in the UAE, transferred from Saudi Arabia and now cooperating; his statements indicate he meant to crash the aircraft in Israel.

Al-Hammami had been suspended as a trainee co-pilot in 2024 after extremist material was found in his possession, and barred from flying by Oman's national carrier. Al-Qaeda imagery and footage of Israeli aircraft appeared on his LinkedIn page within hours of the attack.
global.geopolitical: A man one Gulf state grounded for extremism was flying another's jets. Gulf carriers share crews and airspace but not watchlists, and the gap is now a documented one rather than a theoretical one.
global.socioeconomic: Airlines face the cost of re-screening existing crews, not just applicants, plus pressure to remove or secure crash axes. Israel-bound routes carry a new insurance and staffing premium while the investigation runs.

singapore.headline: Haze pushes central Singapore into unhealthy range as El Niño bites
summary: The 24-hour PSI in the central region crossed into the unhealthy band at 11am on Saturday and peaked at 102, before readings across the island returned to moderate by late evening. NEA said moderate to dense smoke plumes from southern Sumatra were drifting towards Singapore, with additional haze from fires in Kalimantan and hotspot clusters across both.

It is the second unhealthy reading in under three weeks. Experts warned that strong El Niño conditions are likely to delay the end of the dry season to late October or early November, extending the window in which transboundary smoke can reach Singapore.
singapore.geopolitical: Transboundary haze is the one regional problem Singapore cannot solve domestically, and ASEAN's haze agreement has never produced enforcement. A long season tests whether Jakarta's fire-suppression commitments hold under drought.
singapore.socioeconomic: Unhealthy air suppresses outdoor work, construction and F&B trade and pushes clinic visits for respiratory complaints up. A season stretching into November raises the odds of school and workplace advisories, not one-day disruptions.

singapore.headline: Singaporeans cut sugar but 95% now eat too much salt
summary: MOH and HPB released the National Nutrition Survey and population health findings on Saturday. Average daily calorie intake rose from 2,360 in 2019 to 2,460 in 2025, with 57% of residents eating more than their estimated energy needs. A typical portion now carries nearly 10% more calories, as seven in ten residents ate out at least once a day, against six in ten in 2019.

Sodium was the sharper reversal: 95% exceeded the recommended 2,000mg daily limit, up from 88% in 2019. Soupy dishes were the largest contributor among the heaviest consumers at 358mg per 1,000 calories, then processed foods at 266mg. Sugar intake fell, driven by industry reformulation and lower-sugar choices.
singapore.geopolitical: Nothing international here, but the result is a verdict on regulatory design: the sugar levers — Nutri-Grade labels and reformulation — moved the number, while sodium, addressed mainly by persuasion, went backwards.
singapore.socioeconomic: Sodium at these levels loads hypertension, stroke and renal disease onto a super-aged population where 21.4% of citizens are already 65 or older. Expect mandatory sodium labelling, due mid-2027, to be pushed harder.

singapore.headline: Islamic classes of ten or more must register with MUIS, online included
summary: MUIS announced that anyone regularly providing Islamic instruction to ten or more people must register as a Muslim religious school, with the requirement covering lessons conducted online. Officers may inspect registered schools, including by sitting in on classes in person or virtually.

The rules took effect on 2 October. Existing institutions have until 31 March 2027 to comply, and about 50 individuals and organisations are expected to fall within the expanded scope. The tightening follows scrutiny of a religious influencer accused of abuse, and is framed as ensuring instruction comes from qualified, accredited teachers.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is extending a registration regime built for physical madrasahs to online teaching that crosses borders by default, which is where unaccredited instruction now largely reaches Singaporean students.
singapore.socioeconomic: Roughly 50 small providers and freelance teachers face registration, record-keeping and inspection costs, and the ten-person threshold will push some classes below it. Parents gain a verifiable accreditation to check.

singapore.headline: Ride-hailing fuel fees extended to end-November across all four platforms
summary: The National Private Hire Vehicles Association said CDG Zig, Grab, Gojek and Tada have extended their temporary fuel-related driver fees to 30 November. Grab keeps a S$0.90 surcharge on all transport bookings except Standard and metered taxi rides; Gojek a S$0.90 driver fee on all trips.

Tada charges S$0.90 on trips up to S$18 and S$1.20 above S$18.10, while CDG Zig charges S$0.50 on fares below S$15 and S$0.80 at S$15 and above. The platforms pass the money to drivers and take no commission on it. The fees were first introduced as pump prices climbed and have now been rolled over repeatedly.
singapore.geopolitical: This is the G7's diesel problem arriving at a Singapore passenger's checkout screen. Pump prices here track a refined-product market that reserve releases have so far failed to loosen.
singapore.socioeconomic: A S$0.90 add-on is roughly 7% of a typical S$13 fare, and a third rollover makes it a de facto permanent fare rise. Drivers' earnings are held flat rather than improved; passengers absorb the increase.

singapore.headline: Police seize S$39m from sale of Prince Group-linked building
summary: Police seized the proceeds of the sale of 2 Jalan Kilang Barat, a 32,000 sq ft commercial building linked to Cambodia's Prince Group. The property was bought in a private deal by Jackspeed Holdings, a regional automotive firm in motor financing, retail, leasing, insurance and leather upholstery; the money, not the building, was taken.

Investigations into entities and individuals connected to Chen Zhi are continuing. Prince Group is accused of running large-scale online scam compounds staffed by trafficked workers to defraud victims worldwide. Luxury condominiums seized in a separate Singapore money-laundering case drew few buyers at auction earlier this week.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is enforcing against a Cambodian network by taking the cash a willing local buyer paid, which works without extradition or foreign cooperation — the practical limit of unilateral action on regional scam economies.
singapore.socioeconomic: Seizing sale proceeds rather than freezing title lets commercial property change hands and keeps the asset in use, while the forfeiture risk is priced into any future deal involving tainted ownership.

word.definition: A direct vote by an entire electorate on one question, often used to settle a contested issue.
word.etymology: Latin plebiscitum, from plebs "the common people" and scitum "decree", from sciscere "to vote for".
word.example: Sánchez's aides read Saturday's marches as an informal plebiscite on the housing decrees parliament had killed the day before.
